Variability in automated sepsis case detection: a systematic analysis of implementation methods in clinical data repositories.
source: PubMed · Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
desc: [Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA] To systematically review and characterize methodological heterogeneity in sepsis case detection using the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care III (MIMIC-III) and eICU-CRD databases. We conducted a PRISMA-guided systematic review of PubMed and Web of Science (publication years 2016-2024). Studies were eligible if they applied the SOFA-based Sepsis-3 definition to MIMIC-III or eICU-CRD, provided at least one explicit label-calculation detail, reported a traceable detection rate, and met further criteria detailed in the PRISMA flow diagram. We classified each study by study type and unit of analysis (patients, admissions, or ICU stays) and extracted methodological details on sepsis case detection across 6 domains. For studies with available source code, we additionally examined code structure and repository dependencies to identify methodological decisions across these domains. Of 396 publications screened, 64 met inclusion criteria and 12 provided source code. Sepsis detection rates ranged from 3.4% to 65.2% in MIMIC-III and from 9.8% to 47.9% in eICU-CRD. Substantial variability persisted among studies using identical cohort definitions within both databases (MIMIC-III: 16.9%-42.2%; eICU-CRD: 13.9%-31.4%). In a generalized linear mixed model, between-study heterogeneity was extreme (overall τ²≈0.79; 95% prediction interval for a new study's detection rate 5%-63%), and study-level characteristics-including database, study type, infection detection method, code availability, and unit of analysis-explained only a small proportion of this variance (≈9%), with no characteristic reaching statistical significance. The overall proportion of studies reporting methodological details varied by domain: SOFA calculation (53.1%), infection detection methods (42.2%), temporal windows (37.5%), aggregation methods (26.6%), and missing-data handling (17.2%). Source code analysis identified 321 implementation decisions, revealing heterogeneity in baseline SOFA definitions (SOFA = 0 vs dynamic baseline), temporal windows (infection-centered vs ICU-admission-centered) and infection detection methods (antibiotic-culture matching vs APACHE-based diagnosis). Dependencies among several MIMIC-III repositories suggested propagation of implementation decisions across studies. Clinically validated sepsis definitions yield substantially different detection rates across studies using identical datasets. title: Feasibility of Real-Time Integration of a Large Language Model in the EHR to Identify Goals-of-Care Documentation.
source: PubMed · Journal of pain and symptom management
desc: [Journal of pain and symptom management] This article describes integration of a large language model (LLM) into the electronic health record (EHR) to identify unstructured goals-of-care (GOC) documentation or discrete data entry. To determine whether a prompt-engineered LLM reliably detects GOC documentation in clinical notes comparable to human experts and can display this evaluation to clinicians in real time. An interdisciplinary team of palliative care experts created an adjudicated reference standard, which was used to evaluate LLM models in detecting GOC documentation. Given this, the best-fit model (GPT-4o) was then integrated with the EHR for a six-month pilot at four hospitals, then released enterprise-wide. GPT-4o achieved the best performance (specificity 0.95, recall 0.74, precision 0.78). Manual audit on AI-flagged notes (n=325) confirmed substantial expert agreement (86%). In subgroup analyses, there was no statistically significant differences across race, sex, or age (specificity range 0.91-1; all p-values > 0.05). At enterprise scale, the model identified 37,000 patients with GOC documentation within approximately two months. In comparison to those without, patients with AI-flagged GOC documentation had higher acuity rates (ICU stay ≥5 days: 30.2% vs 8.2%; in-hospital mortality: 14.9% vs 0.6%; hospice discharge: 10.5% vs 0.4%). Code status changes were also significantly more frequent (29.3% vs 9.9%; p<0.05). Our initiative met the original objectives by providing a financially sustainable EHR optimization that converts unstructured, high-value GOC narratives into real-time discoverable and trackable documentation. Detecting and displaying these conversations is crucial, increasing clinical situational awareness while reducing documentation burden, leading to enhanced goal-concordant care.

title: Safety, Feasibility, and Acceptability of the MINERVA Voice Conversational Agent for Emergency Department History-Taking
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center; conditions: History Taking, Artificial Intelligence (AI); type: OBSERVATIONAL; enrollment: 250; status: ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION] This study evaluates whether an artificial intelligence (AI) conversational agent called MINERVA (Medical Interface for Navigating the Emergency Room with Voice Assistance) can safely and feasibly gather medical histories from emergency department (ED) patients and produce accurate summaries. The main questions it aims to answer are: Can an AI conversational agent gather and summarize patient histories in the emergency department? Are the resulting summaries accurate? Do they capture essential clinical information? Can an AI agent overseeing these conversations independently identify red-flag symptoms that may need time-sensitive clinical interventions? Adult ED patients interact with MINERVA via either voice chat or typing on a keyboard. MINERVA asks them questions about their symptoms and generates a summary which the patients review for accuracy. MINERVA reviews the conversation for clinical red flags that suggest urgent evaluation is required. Participants fill out a survey providing feedback on their experience. The summary is not saved in the medical record and clinical care is not affected. Physician reviewers will evaluate the safety, accuracy, and clinical value of the MINERVA interview transcripts and summaries using standardized rubrics, including whether MINERVA was correct in identifying red-flag symptoms that may need time-sensitive clinical interventions.

title: Design and Technical Evaluation of a Standards-Based System That Delivers Enclave-Derived Case-Finding Models to Patients and Clinicians
desc: BackgroundResearch data enclaves such as the All of Us Research Program do not allow participant-level data, or models fitted to them, to leave, which makes it hard to deliver case-finding models, which flag patients with possibly uncoded conditions for clinician review, to patients and clinicians. ObjectivesWe describe and technically evaluate a system that fits models outside an enclave from released summary counts and delivers them through standard health information technology interfaces. MethodsWe exported dissemination-compliant summary counts from the All of Us Researcher Workbench and, outside the enclave, fitted versioned models for Long COVID, chronic fatigue, fibromyalgia, endometriosis, Lyme disease, lupus, migraine, depression, and anxiety. A model contract (a model file and a written specification), a Python reference implementation, and synthetic Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) test patients define the expected outputs. One JavaScript scorer runs in a patient demonstration, a SMART on FHIR clinician application, and a CDS Hooks service. An atlas displays aggregate results. We evaluated the system on synthetic records with automated tests, cross-implementation output comparison, launches through the public SMART sandbox, and a counterexample review of the scoring and display rules. ResultsThe deployed Long COVID model had an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.67 in a random validation split. The eight self-report models reached 0.61 to 0.82 in identifying self-reporters without a code. The JavaScript scorer reproduced all 162 reference outputs exactly, and all 437 automated tests passed. A counterexample review found 5 classes of failure, including scoring ineligible patients and treating unavailable data as absent, all fixed and added as tests. ConclusionsModels fitted from released summary counts can be delivered through FHIR, SMART on FHIR, and CDS Hooks with reproducible scoring on synthetic records. Real-record interoperability, usability, and prospective clinical performance remain to be evaluated.

title: Targeting PRMT5 Across Cancers and AI-Driven Discovery of Candidate Compounds
desc: Protein arginine methyltransferase 5 (PRMT5) is a promising anticancer target, yet existing inhibitors shown limited clinical efficacy. Here, we paired multi-omics pan-cancer profiling with a machine learning virtual screening pipeline. Bioinformatics analyses with TIMER3, GEPIA2, UALCAN/CPTAC, the Human Protein Atlas, cBioPortal, STRING and Enrichr revealed widespread of PRMT5 mRNA expression, protein abundance, survival, genetic alteration, immune infiltration and co-expression networks with tumor-specific prognostic impact in GBM, LGG and KIRC. A deep neural network screened about 1.5 million PubChem compounds and deep neural network reached a ROC-AUC = 0.9857 and prioritized three candidates, CID 44345182, CID 2794188 and CID 44345334. Subsequent molecular docking against PRMT5 (PDB ID: 4X61), ADMET filtering and toxicity prediction, and 100 ns molecular dynamics (MD) simulations identified CID 44345182 as the potential hit, similar the docking scores of -9.8 compared with -9.2 kcal/mol for the reference ligand in binding affinity and trajectory stability. These findings clarify the context-dependent roles of PRMT5 and further experiment validations are needed to establish CID 44345182 as a promising candidate.

title: Toward Automated Detection of Documentation Inconsistencies in Electronic Health Records
desc: Objective:To characterize the kinds of internal documentation inconsistencies a general-domain large language model (LLM) can surface from real-world discharge summaries, and to identify recurring failure modes that limit reliability at scale. Materials and Methods: We applied a two-stage LLM pipeline---open-ended candidate identification (Gemini 2.5 Pro) followed by context-grounded verification (Gemini 2.5 Flash)---to 3000 MIMIC-IV-Note discharge summaries drawn as three contiguous 1000-note batches from distinct positions in the corpus. Two clinicians independently reviewed a domain-stratified sample of 268 retained candidates; a third adjudicated disagreements. Results: Stage~1 proposed 11333 candidates; 3461 were retained after Stage~2 verification---machine-generated candidates---with at least one in 69.7% of admissions.
